_readme: VERIFIED TERMS — highest-precedence source for the glossary bundle.
Every entry here was checked against a primary or authoritative source: the RFC, the W3C/WHATWG
spec, the paper that introduced the idea, or the vendor's own reference. The `source` field records
which one, and `sourceUrl` is where it was read.
THE RULE THIS FILE EXISTS TO ENFORCE: the estate is the DISCOVERY source, never the AUTHORITY
source. Session transcripts, emails, memory files and repo docs tell us WHICH terms are worth having.
They never tell us what a term MEANS. Anything whose meaning cannot be traced to a source below
does not get an entry — an unverifiable entry is worse than an absent one.
`misread` is optional and holds the common wrong understanding, stated plainly. It is more useful
to a newcomer than a third restatement of the right answer.
Adding a term: verify first, cite second, write third. Never the other way round.

terms.desc: The request/response protocol the web runs on. A client asks for something, a server answers. HTTP is stateless: the protocol itself remembers nothing between requests, which is why sessions have to be rebuilt on every call using cookies or tokens.
terms.source: RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, June 2022), §1.1

terms.desc: The HTTP method that asks a server to process the data you are sending, according to whatever that particular resource does with it. POST is deliberately open-ended — the spec does not say it means "create".
terms.misread: That POST always means "create a record". The spec only says the server processes the submitted data by its own rules; creating is one common case, not the definition.
terms.source: RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, June 2022), §9.3.3

terms.desc: The HTTP method that asks a server to create or replace a resource's entire state with the data you sent. Unlike POST, it is idempotent: sending it twice leaves the same result as sending it once.
terms.source: RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, June 2022), §9.3.4

terms.desc: The HTTP method that asks the origin server to remove a resource.
terms.source: RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, June 2022), §9.3.5

terms.desc: A property of a request method: doing it many times has the same intended effect on the server as doing it once. It is what makes a client safe to retry after a timeout, because a duplicate cannot do extra damage.
terms.misread: That idempotent means "returns the same answer every time". It is about the effect on the server, not the response you get back.
terms.source: RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, June 2022), §9.2.2

terms.desc: An HTTP method whose defined meaning is essentially read-only — it does not alter server state. GET and HEAD are the everyday examples, which is why crawlers and prefetchers may call them freely.
terms.source: RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (IETF, June 2022), §9.2.1

terms.desc: The transport protocol that turns an unreliable network into a reliable, in-order stream of bytes. It detects lost packets using sequence numbers and corrupted ones using checksums, then retransmits. Connections are set up by a three-way handshake before any data moves.
terms.source: RFC 9293, "Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)" (IETF, August 2022) — obsoletes RFC 793

terms.desc: The protocol that protects traffic between two applications over the internet — the S in HTTPS. It provides three things: the server is authenticated (so you know who you are talking to), the data is confidential, and tampering is detectable.
terms.misread: That TLS only encrypts. Authentication and integrity matter just as much — encryption alone would still let an impostor answer you.
terms.source: RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3" (IETF, August 2018)

terms.desc: The distributed directory that turns names into addresses, so that a name does not have to carry any routing information inside it. It has three parts: the tree-shaped namespace and its records, the name servers that hold the data, and the resolvers that go and fetch it. It replaced a single shared HOSTS.TXT file that stopped scaling in the 1980s.
terms.source: RFC 1034, "Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities" (IETF, November 1987)

terms.desc: A compact string that identifies a resource, abstract or physical. URI is the general category; URL is the subset that also tells you how to reach the thing. The spec's own advice is to say "URI" rather than "URL" or "URN" in new writing.
terms.source: RFC 3986, "Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax" (IETF, January 2005)

terms.desc: The subset of URIs that, as well as identifying a resource, describes how to get to it — its access mechanism or network location. Every URL is a URI; not every URI is a URL.
terms.misread: That URL and URI are interchangeable. They are nested, not equal: URL is the narrower term.
terms.source: RFC 3986, "Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax" (IETF, January 2005), §1.1.3

terms.desc: A URI under the "urn" scheme, meant to stay globally unique and persistent as a name even after the thing it names is gone or unreachable. It identifies without locating.
terms.source: RFC 3986, "Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax" (IETF, January 2005), §1.1.3

terms.desc: A protocol giving a browser and a server one persistent, two-way connection, so either side can send at any time. It exists because the alternative — repeatedly opening HTTP connections to poll for news — was wasteful and awkward.
terms.source: RFC 6455, "The WebSocket Protocol" (IETF, December 2011)

terms.desc: A browser feature letting a server push messages to a page over an ordinary HTTP response, using the EventSource interface and the text/event-stream format. One direction only, server to page — that is the trade against WebSocket, and it is why SSE is simpler.
terms.misread: That SSE is its own protocol. It is an API and a wire format defined in the HTML Standard, carried over plain HTTP.
terms.source: WHATWG HTML Standard, "Server-sent events"

terms.desc: The protocol by which a server tells a browser that a page from another origin is allowed to read its response. If a resource does not speak CORS, the browser returns a network error instead of the data. GET, HEAD and POST are "safelisted" methods; anything else triggers a preflight check first.
terms.misread: That CORS is a restriction someone imposed on you. It is the mechanism for granting cross-origin access — the restriction is the browser's same-origin policy, which CORS exists to relax.
terms.source: WHATWG Fetch Standard, §3.2 CORS protocol

terms.desc: A compact, URL-safe way to carry a set of claims — statements about a subject — as a JSON object between two parties. The claims are encoded so they can be signed, MACed, or encrypted.
terms.misread: That a JWT is encrypted and therefore private. The common signed form (JWS) is only signed: anyone holding the token can read every claim inside it. Encryption is a separate, less-used form (JWE).
terms.source: RFC 7519, "JSON Web Token (JWT)" (IETF, May 2015), Terminology

terms.desc: A framework that lets a third-party application get limited access to a service on your behalf without you handing over your password. Instead of credentials, the app receives an access token carrying a specific scope and lifetime.
terms.misread: That OAuth logs you in. It is an authorization framework — it delegates access to resources. The spec explicitly puts how the user is authenticated outside its own scope. Logging in on top of OAuth is a separate layer (OpenID Connect).
terms.source: RFC 6749, "The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework" (IETF, October 2012)

terms.desc: An addition to OAuth 2.0 that stops an intercepted authorization code from being useful to whoever grabbed it. The client commits to a secret at the start and must prove it at the end. Pronounced "pixy". It was written for public clients such as mobile apps, where another app on the same device can intercept the redirect.
terms.source: RFC 7636, "Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients" (IETF, September 2015)

terms.desc: An attack where a site is tricked into sending an attacker's script to another user's browser. Because the browser believes the script came from a site it trusts, the script runs with that trust and can reach cookies and session tokens.
terms.misread: That a read-only or purely informational site cannot be seriously hurt by XSS. OWASP calls this out directly — reflected XSS can be severe on sites with no accounts and no transactions.
terms.source: OWASP, "Cross Site Scripting (XSS)"

terms.desc: An attack that makes a logged-in user's browser fire off a request they never intended, using the session they already have. The attacker never sees the response — they just cause the action.
terms.misread: That CSRF and XSS are the same family of bug. XSS injects and runs a script in the victim's browser; CSRF runs no script of its own, it just abuses an existing login. XSS can be used to defeat CSRF defences, which is why they get conflated.
terms.source: OWASP, "Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)"

terms.desc: An attack where the attacker makes the *server* fetch a URL of their choosing, reaching internal resources the attacker could never reach directly — cloud metadata endpoints, internal databases, local files.
terms.misread: That the leading S makes it a variant of CSRF. The forged request comes from the server, not the victim's browser, and the payoff is internal network access rather than an unwanted user action.
terms.source: OWASP, "Server Side Request Forgery"

terms.desc: A way to prove a message came from someone holding a shared secret key and has not been altered, by combining that key with a hash function. It authenticates; it does not hide anything.
terms.misread: That HMAC encrypts. It produces a verification tag alongside the message — the message itself stays readable.
terms.source: NIST FIPS 198-1, "The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC)" (February 2009); construction defined in RFC 2104

terms.desc: The dominant text encoding: one to four bytes per character, covering the whole Unicode range. Its decisive property is that plain ASCII text is already valid UTF-8 unchanged, so older tools kept working — which is most of why it won.
terms.misread: That the 8 means eight bits per character. It is the code unit size; characters take one to four of them.
terms.source: RFC 3629, "UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646" (IETF, November 2003)

terms.desc: The standard operating-system interface — system calls, a shell, and the common command-line utilities — that lets source code be written once and compiled on any conforming system. The current edition is IEEE Std 1003.1-2024 (Open Group Base Specifications, Issue 8).
terms.misread: That POSIX compliance means compiled programs are portable. It is portability at the *source* level; binary portability is explicitly out of scope.
terms.source: The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8, IEEE Std 1003.1-2024, Base Definitions §1 (Scope)

terms.desc: The timestamp format used across internet protocols — 2026-08-16T14:30:00Z — defined as a deliberately narrow profile of ISO 8601. Every time carries a stated offset from UTC, and the Z suffix means an offset of exactly 00:00. It exists because full ISO 8601 is too permissive to interoperate on.
terms.source: RFC 3339, "Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps" (IETF, July 2002)

terms.desc: The reference time scale that all internet timestamps state their offset from. A trailing Z on a timestamp means the offset is zero — the time is already in UTC.
terms.source: RFC 3339, "Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps" (IETF, July 2002), §1–2

terms.desc: The W3C's recommendation for making web content accessible, organised into testable success criteria at three conformance levels. WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 12 December 2024.
terms.misread: That reaching the top level makes a site accessible to everyone. The guidelines say plainly that even AAA content will not be accessible to people with all types, degrees or combinations of disability, particularly cognitive, language and learning disabilities.
terms.source: W3C, "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2", W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024

terms.desc: The middle of WCAG's three conformance levels — A is lowest, AA next, AAA highest. AA is the level most public-sector accessibility rules point at, which is why it is the one usually quoted.
terms.source: W3C, "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2", Conformance

terms.desc: The four principles WCAG is built on. Content must be presentable in a way users can perceive; the interface must be operable; content and operation must be understandable; and it must be robust enough to keep working across technologies and assistive tools.
terms.source: W3C, "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2", WCAG 2 Layers of Guidance

terms.desc: A set of HTML attributes that tell assistive technology what a component *is* and what state it is in, for interfaces built out of generic elements. WAI-ARIA 1.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 6 June 2023.
terms.misread: That adding ARIA makes a component behave correctly. It changes semantics only — nothing in the DOM changes, just the accessibility tree. Keyboard handling and focus management remain entirely yours to write.
terms.source: W3C, "Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2", W3C Recommendation 6 June 2023

terms.desc: The programming interface that represents a loaded page as a tree of nodes and objects, so code can read and change its structure, style and content.
terms.misread: That the DOM is part of JavaScript. It is a separate, language-independent Web API. Node.js runs JavaScript with no DOM at all, and the DOM can be driven from other languages.
terms.source: MDN Web Docs, "Introduction to the DOM" (Mozilla)

terms.desc: A CSS colour function that specifies an Oklab colour by lightness, chroma and hue. Oklab is a device-independent colour space, so equal numeric steps look like equal visual steps — unlike HSL, where changing only the hue visibly changes the brightness too.
terms.source: W3C, "CSS Color Module Level 4", Candidate Recommendation Draft 6 August 2026, §9

terms.desc: A named design decision — at minimum a name and a value, such as color-text-primary: #000000 — stored in a tool-neutral JSON file so design tools and code can share one source of truth.
terms.misread: That the DTCG format is a settled standard. It is a Draft Community Group Report, not a W3C Standard, and the draft itself says not to treat that version as authoritative.
terms.source: Design Tokens Community Group, "Design Tokens Format Module", Draft Community Group Report 30 July 2026

terms.desc: A JSON file holding a web application's metadata — name, icons, start URL, display mode, orientation, scope — so a browser can install and launch it like a native app.
terms.source: W3C, "Web Application Manifest", W3C Working Draft 13 August 2026

terms.desc: An industry term for a website built to install and behave like a native app, typically using a Web App Manifest and a service worker.
terms.misread: That PWA is a W3C standard you can conform to. It is not defined by any specification — the underlying pieces (manifest, service workers) are standardised, but "PWA" itself is community terminology with no formal conformance criteria.
terms.source: W3C, "Web Application Manifest" (W3C Working Draft 13 August 2026) — the manifest is specified; the term PWA is not defined there

terms.desc: The neural network architecture nearly every modern language model is built on. Its point was subtractive: it dispensed with recurrence and convolutions entirely and relied on attention alone, which is what made training parallelisable at scale.
terms.source: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", arXiv:1706.03762 (June 2017)

terms.desc: A language representation model that pre-trains on unlabelled text while conditioning on both left and right context in every layer. That two-sided view is what set it apart from the left-to-right models before it.
terms.source: Devlin et al., "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding", arXiv:1810.04805 (October 2018)

terms.desc: A way of splitting text into subword pieces by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair, borrowed from a compression algorithm. It makes vocabulary open-ended: a word never seen in training is represented as a sequence of smaller known pieces instead of being lost.
terms.source: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch, "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units", arXiv:1508.07909 (August 2015; ACL 2016)

terms.desc: Combining a model's built-in (parametric) knowledge with an external, searchable store it retrieves from at answer time. The original work paired a pre-trained seq2seq model with a dense vector index of Wikipedia. The gains it claimed were as much about provenance and updatable knowledge as about accuracy.
terms.source: Lewis et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks", arXiv:2005.11401 (May 2020)

terms.desc: A fine-tuning method that freezes the pre-trained weights and injects small trainable rank-decomposition matrices into each Transformer layer. On GPT-3 175B the paper reports 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and 3× less GPU memory than full fine-tuning.
terms.source: Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models", arXiv:2106.09685 (June 2021)

terms.desc: Training a model on what people actually preferred rather than on text alone: collect demonstrations and fine-tune on them, then collect rankings of the model's own outputs and fine-tune again with reinforcement learning against those rankings. In the InstructGPT work a 1.3B model tuned this way was preferred to 175B GPT-3 — a hundred times larger.
terms.source: Ouyang et al., "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback", arXiv:2203.02155 (March 2022)

terms.desc: An alternative to RLHF that reparameterises the reward model so the optimal policy has a closed form, turning alignment into a simple classification loss. It needs no separate reward model and no sampling from the model during fine-tuning, which is why it is described as lighter and more stable than the RL pipeline it replaces.
terms.source: Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model", arXiv:2305.18290 (May 2023)

terms.desc: A variant of PPO introduced with DeepSeekMath that improves mathematical reasoning while cutting PPO's memory use.
terms.note: Deliberately narrow: this is the full extent of what the paper's abstract states. Claims about how it treats the critic or computes its baseline were not verifiable from the abstract and are omitted rather than guessed.
terms.source: Shao et al., "DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models", arXiv:2402.03300 (February 2024), abstract

terms.desc: An attention algorithm that manages a model's key-value cache the way an operating system manages virtual memory — in pages. This stops the cache fragmenting and lets separate requests share pages.
terms.source: Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", arXiv:2309.06180 (September 2023)

terms.desc: An LLM serving system built on PagedAttention, aimed at wasting as little key-value cache memory as possible and sharing it flexibly between requests. The paper reports 2–4× the throughput of comparable systems at the same latency.
terms.source: Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", arXiv:2309.06180 (September 2023)

terms.desc: The per-request memory a serving system keeps so it does not recompute attention over the whole conversation on every new token. It is large and it grows and shrinks unpredictably, so mismanaging it — through fragmentation and duplication — is what limits how many requests a GPU can serve at once.
terms.source: Kwon et al., "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention", arXiv:2309.06180 (September 2023)

terms.desc: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and programming model for running general-purpose work on the GPU. It is a platform and a model, not a language — it works through extensions to existing languages and its own compiler.
terms.misread: That CUDA stands for "Compute Unified Device Architecture". NVIDIA's current programming guide defines CUDA without expanding it at all; the expansion is legacy and no longer used by the vendor.
terms.source: NVIDIA, "CUDA C++ Programming Guide", Introduction

terms.desc: A single-file binary format for model weights, built for fast loading in ggml-based inference engines such as llama.cpp. Unlike tensor-only formats it stores its metadata as typed key-value pairs alongside the tensors, which is what lets a file describe its own architecture. Created by Georgi Gerganov as the successor to the earlier GGML, GGMF and GGJT formats.
terms.misread: That GGUF is Ollama's format. Ollama consumes it; it comes from the ggml/llama.cpp project. The commonly quoted expansion "GGML Unified Format" appears nowhere in the format specification.
terms.source: ggml project, "GGUF" specification (docs/gguf.md); Hugging Face Hub documentation, "GGUF"

terms.desc: A common language for describing machine-learning models as computation graphs, so a model trained in one framework can be deployed by a runtime built for another. It exists to spare teams a separate deployment path per framework.
terms.source: ONNX documentation, "ONNX Concepts"

terms.desc: An open standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems — data sources, tools and prompt workflows — so an integration is written once and works across every client that speaks it. Its own documentation likens it to USB-C for AI applications.
terms.source: Model Context Protocol documentation, "What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?"

terms.desc: A framework for remote procedure calls: client code calls a method on a server on another machine as though it were a local object. Services and their methods are declared up front, and by default the wire format is Protocol Buffers rather than JSON.
terms.misread: That the g stands for Google. The official documentation does not expand it — the letter's meaning has changed with each release.
terms.source: gRPC documentation, "Introduction to gRPC"

terms.desc: Google's language- and platform-neutral format for serialising structured data. You declare the shape once in a .proto file and it generates native code for each language. Smaller and faster on the wire than JSON, and designed so a schema can evolve without breaking data already written.
terms.source: Google, "Protocol Buffers Overview"

terms.desc: A protocol that lets one language server provide completion, diagnostics and navigation to any editor that speaks it, over JSON-RPC. It exists to kill the M×N problem: before it, every language had to be reimplemented separately for every editor.
terms.source: Microsoft, "Language Server Protocol" — Overview

terms.desc: The Linux Foundation body that publishes the open standards for container formats and runtimes, founded in 2015 by Docker, CoreOS and others. It maintains three specifications: runtime, image and distribution.
terms.misread: In cloud writing OCI also abbreviates Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, an unrelated thing. Which one is meant has to come from context.
terms.source: Open Container Initiative, "About / Overview"

terms.desc: A versioning convention where MAJOR increments on incompatible API changes, MINOR on backward-compatible additions, and PATCH on backward-compatible bug fixes.
terms.misread: That a version number always carries those promises. Under major version zero (0.y.z) the spec says anything may change at any time and the public API should not be considered stable — so 0.x carries no compatibility guarantee at all.
terms.source: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0

terms.desc: A short permissive open-source licence: anyone may use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software, provided the copyright notice and licence text travel with it. The software is supplied as-is, with all warranties disclaimed.
terms.misread: That MIT is an acronym. It is named after the institution where it originated; the OSI licence text expands nothing.
terms.source: Open Source Initiative, "The MIT License"

terms.desc: A journalling mode that inverts the usual arrangement: instead of copying the old data aside and writing changes into the database, the original stays put and changes are appended to a separate WAL file, with a commit recorded by appending a marker. Readers and a writer can then proceed at the same time. In SQLite it has been available since version 3.7.0 (2010).
terms.misread: That WAL is strictly faster. SQLite lists real costs: it will not work over a network filesystem because it needs shared memory between processes, read-heavy workloads can be marginally slower, and very large transactions are usually better off in rollback mode.
terms.source: SQLite documentation, "Write-Ahead Logging"

terms.desc: SQLite's full-text search extension, implemented as a virtual table module. It indexes text columns and answers phrase, prefix, proximity (NEAR) and boolean queries via the MATCH operator, ranking results with BM25 by default.
terms.source: SQLite documentation, "SQLite FTS5 Extension"

terms.desc: A relevance ranking function for full-text search, used as the default ranking in SQLite's FTS5. In that implementation a numerically lower score means a better match, so results sort best-first in ascending order.
terms.note: Scoped to what was verifiable from SQLite's documentation. The originating information-retrieval literature was not reachable during verification, so no claim is made here about the formula or the meaning of "BM".
terms.source: SQLite documentation, "SQLite FTS5 Extension" — Sorting by Auxiliary Function Results
